newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish police widen Russia shipping murder probe.
newsitem.headline: Swedish police widen Russia shipping murder probe.

text.p: Swedish police investigating possible involvement of Russian mafia in a recent murder said on Friday they had widened the investigation to two other killings in Sweden with victims linked to Russian shipping.

Russian businessman Evgueni Goloubtchik, 46, was shot several times by a masked man on a mountain bike as he was loading a car at a shopping centre in Malmo, in southern Sweden, last Saturday. He died in front of his 15-year-old son.
Despite hundreds of witnesses, police have been unable to track down the killer.
Police spokesman Hans Strindlund said the murder appeared to have been a professional job and similar to two other unsolved murders in Stockholm last year.
All three murders were carried out in open, public places in broad daylight with the victims shot in the head.
All three victims were involved in some way with the Russian shipping industry.
"The murders were very professional, very cold and calculated," Strindlund told Reuters.
"It must also be more than a coincidence that all three were involved in the Russia shipping business."
Goloubtchik, who moved to Malmo with his family in 1994, was one of the owners of a newly established shipping company, NB Shipping Services, based in Malmo.
Malmo police spokesman Torsten Elofsson said Goloubtchik had also been an agent for Russia's Murmansk Shipping Company but had broken his ties with this company recently.
The murders in Stockholm happened last September.

On September 16 a 37-year-old Swedish metal dealer from southern Stockholm with links to Russian shipping was shot in the head. His body was found two days later in a hire car left in a car park at Upplands Bro, north of Stockholm.
The day he was found, a 45-year-old Polish man was murdered in Stockholm, also shot in the head.

Strindlund said the Polish man had been involved with the Ilyich ferry which was seized from Russia's Baltic Shipping Company in late 1995 as the company owed its creditors about 70 million Swedish crowns ($8.5 million).
The victim had first fought against the court's sale of the ferry but later signed the papers when the ship was sold in the autumn of 1996 to repay the shipping line's debt, Strindlund said.
"These murders appear to be carried out by hitmen. We have not seen this kind of thing in Sweden before," Strindlund said.
He said police had seen increasing involvement of Russians in crime in Stockholm and elsewhere in Sweden in recent years, ranging from gold trading to prostitution.
